en.statement: In the OWASP Top 10:2025, the list names ten individual CWE weaknesses, one per entry.
en.explanation: The 2025 entries are categories that group multiple CWEs under a common name, partly because common vulnerabilities such as Injection or Hardcoded Passwords are described by several CWEs.

en.statement: In the OWASP Top 10:2025, the revision adds two new categories and consolidates one former category.
en.explanation: The 2025 Introduction describes the revision as two new categories and one consolidation.

en.statement: In the OWASP Top 10:2025, A01:2025 Broken Access Control shares the list with a standalone SSRF category.
en.explanation: The 2025 Introduction folds Server-Side Request Forgery into A01:2025 Broken Access Control. SSRF has no standalone 2025 entry.

en.statement: In the OWASP Top 10:2025, A02:2025 Security Misconfiguration ranks higher than in 2021.
en.explanation: A02:2025 Security Misconfiguration moves from fifth in the 2021 edition to second in 2025.

en.statement: In the OWASP Top 10:2025, A03:2025 Software Supply Chain Failures narrows the scope of A06:2021.
en.explanation: A03:2025 Software Supply Chain Failures expands A06:2021 Vulnerable and Outdated Components to include dependencies, build systems, and distribution.

en.statement: In the OWASP Top 10:2025, A04:2025 Cryptographic Failures moves higher than its 2021 rank.
en.explanation: A04:2025 Cryptographic Failures falls from second in the 2021 edition to fourth in 2025.

en.statement: In the OWASP Top 10:2025, A05:2025 Injection keeps its 2021 ranking.
en.explanation: A05:2025 Injection moves from third in the 2021 edition to fifth in 2025.

en.statement: In the OWASP Top 10:2025, A06:2025 Insecure Design ranks lower than in 2021.
en.explanation: A06:2025 Insecure Design moves down two positions from its fourth-place rank in 2021.

en.statement: In the OWASP Top 10:2025, A08:2025 Software or Data Integrity Failures stays at eighth place.
en.explanation: A08:2025 Software or Data Integrity Failures retains the eighth position from the 2021 edition.

en.statement: In the OWASP Top 10:2025, A10:2025 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions enters as a new category.
en.explanation: A10:2025 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions is new in 2025 and covers security failures arising from abnormal conditions.

en.statement: In the OWASP Top 10:2025, A01:2025 Broken Access Control lets client-side route guards secure API access.
en.explanation: Client-side checks are bypassable. A01 says trusted server-side code or serverless APIs need to enforce access control.

source.title: A01 Broken Access Control - OWASP Top 10:2025

en.statement: In the OWASP Top 10:2025, A07:2025 Authentication Failures includes Cross-Site Request Forgery.
en.explanation: The 2025 Top 10 places Cross-Site Request Forgery under A01:2025 Broken Access Control.

source.title: A01 Broken Access Control - OWASP Top 10:2025

en.statement: In the OWASP Top 10:2025, A01:2025 Broken Access Control includes API exposure from permissive CORS settings.
en.explanation: A01 identifies CORS misconfiguration that permits API access from unauthorized or untrusted origins.

source.title: A01 Broken Access Control - OWASP Top 10:2025

en.statement: In the OWASP Top 10:2025, A02:2025 Security Misconfiguration includes missing security response headers.
en.explanation: A02 includes absent or insecure security headers and recommends sending security directives to clients.

en.statement: In the OWASP Top 10:2025, A02:2025 Security Misconfiguration describes servers returning stack traces to users.
en.explanation: A02 counts error handling that returns stack traces or other overly informative messages to users as misconfiguration, and advises central interception of such messages.

en.statement: In the OWASP Top 10:2025, A03:2025 Software Supply Chain Failures advises rebuilding artifacts per environment.
en.explanation: A03 advises promoting the same artifact through environments instead of rebuilding it, keeping builds immutable and backing integrity with provenance, signing and time stamping.

en.statement: In the OWASP Top 10:2025, A03:2025 Software Supply Chain Failures includes weakly secured CI/CD pipelines.
en.explanation: A03 includes CI/CD pipelines whose security is weaker than the systems they build and deploy.

source.title: A03 Software Supply Chain Failures - OWASP Top 10:2025

en.statement: In the OWASP Top 10:2025, A04:2025 Cryptographic Failures accepts CDN caching of sensitive responses over TLS.
en.explanation: A04 says to disable caching of responses that contain sensitive data, including CDN, web server and application caches such as Redis, whatever the transport encryption.

en.statement: In the OWASP Top 10:2025, Cross-site Scripting falls under the A05:2025 Injection category.
en.explanation: A05:2025 Injection explicitly includes Cross-site Scripting among the weaknesses in the category.

en.statement: In the OWASP Top 10:2025, A06:2025 Insecure Design calls for threat modeling around business logic.
en.explanation: A06 calls for threat modeling in critical application flows, including business logic and access control, during design.

en.statement: In the OWASP Top 10:2025, A06:2025 Insecure Design is described as the source of the other nine risk categories.
en.explanation: OWASP states that insecure design is not the source of all other Top Ten categories; it means missing or ineffective control design, which a perfect implementation cannot fix.

en.statement: In the OWASP Top 10:2025, A07:2025 Authentication Failures flags session IDs placed in URLs as unsafe.
en.explanation: A07 lists session identifiers in URLs as a weakness and recommends keeping them in secure cookies instead.

en.statement: In the OWASP Top 10:2025, A07:2025 Authentication Failures recommends a new random session ID after login.
en.explanation: A07 recommends a server-side session manager that generates a new, random, high-entropy session ID after login.

en.statement: In the OWASP Top 10:2025, A08:2025 Software or Data Integrity Failures uses signatures to verify updates.
en.explanation: A08 recommends digital signatures or similar checks to confirm an update's expected source and detect modification.

source.title: A08 Software or Data Integrity Failures - OWASP Top 10:2025

en.statement: In the OWASP Top 10:2025, insecure deserialization of client-sent state falls under A05:2025 Injection.
en.explanation: A08:2025 Software or Data Integrity Failures covers insecure deserialization: serialized data an attacker can see and modify needs an integrity check or digital signature before use.

source.title: A08:2025 Software or Data Integrity Failures

en.statement: In the OWASP Top 10:2025, A09:2025 Security Logging and Alerting Failures keeps logs solely on the app server.
en.explanation: A09 lists logs stored only locally and lacking proper backup as a security logging failure.

source.title: A09 Security Logging and Alerting Failures - OWASP Top 10:2025

en.statement: In the OWASP Top 10:2025, A10:2025 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions calls for rolling back failed transactions.
en.explanation: A10 advises rolling back every part of an interrupted transaction and starting again, a fail-closed response.

source.title: A10 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions - OWASP Top 10:2025

en.statement: In the OWASP Top 10:2025, A10:2025 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions covers only conditions that crash the app.
en.explanation: A10 covers an app that fails to prevent an unusual situation, fails to identify it as it happens, or responds poorly afterwards; crashes are one possible result among unexpected behavior and vulnerabilities.

en.statement: A script-created about:blank popup gets an opaque origin separate from its creator.
en.explanation: A script-created about:blank document inherits the origin of the document that created it.

en.statement: A browser can treat sibling subdomains as the same site through their registrable domain.
en.explanation: Site comparison uses the registrable domain, which can group sibling subdomains under one site.

en.statement: The same-origin policy typically blocks images embedded from another origin.
en.explanation: Cross-origin embedding is typically permitted; an img element can display an image hosted on another origin.

en.statement: A 200 status alone lets script read the body of a cross-origin fetch() response.
en.explanation: The status code plays no part: the same-origin policy keeps a cross-origin response body from script unless the response passes the CORS check.

en.statement: A script can read window.closed on a referenced Window from another origin.
en.explanation: The limited cross-origin Window API permits scripts to read window.closed.

en.statement: A script can read location.href on a Window from another origin.
en.explanation: For a cross-origin Location, location.href is write-only. A script can navigate the other window but cannot read its URL.

en.statement: window.postMessage lets documents on different origins exchange messages.
en.explanation: window.postMessage provides cross-origin document messaging; receivers should check the sender's origin.

en.statement: A browser separates Web Storage and IndexedDB data by origin.
en.explanation: Web Storage and IndexedDB allocate data by origin, so a script from one origin cannot access another origin's store.

en.statement: Changing document.domain also changes the origin checks for localStorage.
en.explanation: The deprecated document.domain setter does not relax the origin checks used by localStorage.

en.statement: A specific Access-Control-Allow-Origin value names the origin whose JavaScript may read the response.
en.explanation: The resource server uses this response header to identify an origin whose scripts the browser may expose the response to.

en.statement: A browser sends the actual request method as the method of a CORS preflight.
en.explanation: The browser sends an OPTIONS request for the preflight. It sends the actual request method after the preflight succeeds.

en.statement: A cross-origin fetch() using the PUT method triggers a CORS preflight.
en.explanation: PUT falls outside the methods allowed for cross-origin requests that avoid a preflight.

en.statement: A preflight response uses Access-Control-Allow-Headers to approve custom headers in the actual request.
en.explanation: The server lists request header names it permits in Access-Control-Allow-Headers.

en.statement: Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true makes fetch() attach cookies to a cross-origin request.
en.explanation: Access-Control-Allow-Credentials controls exposure of a credentialed response. The request's credentials mode governs whether fetch() includes credentials.

en.statement: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * exposes a credentialed response to JavaScript.
en.explanation: A browser blocks script access to a credentialed response when Access-Control-Allow-Origin has the wildcard value. The server needs an explicit origin.

en.statement: Page script reads a cross-origin CORS response's Content-Type header by default.
en.explanation: Content-Type is a CORS-safelisted response header, exposed to page scripts like Cache-Control and Content-Length; any other response header needs Access-Control-Expose-Headers.

en.statement: A failed CORS check can tell page JavaScript which response header caused the failure.
en.explanation: JavaScript receives a generic CORS failure. The browser console provides the specific reason for debugging.

en.statement: CORS response headers decide whether a command-line HTTP client receives a server response.
en.explanation: Browsers enforce CORS when page code accesses cross-origin responses. A command-line HTTP client does not enforce those browser access checks.

en.statement: HttpOnly keeps a cookie out of JavaScript-initiated fetch() requests.
en.explanation: HttpOnly prevents access through JavaScript APIs such as Document.cookie. An eligible fetch() request still sends the cookie.

en.statement: A cookie with Domain=example.com excludes subdomains of example.com.
en.explanation: Domain=example.com makes the cookie available to example.com and its subdomains. Omitting Domain creates a host-only cookie.

en.statement: Path=/docs sends a cookie to /docs and paths beneath it.
en.explanation: Path matches the requested URL path, including matching subpaths such as /docs/Web.

en.statement: Expires decides a cookie's lifetime when Expires and Max-Age appear together.
en.explanation: Max-Age takes precedence over Expires when a cookie has both attributes.

en.statement: SameSite=Strict withholds a cookie when the user follows a link from another site.
en.explanation: Strict sends a cookie only on requests that originate from the site that set it, so a top-level navigation started from another site's link arrives without the Strict cookie.

en.statement: SameSite=None requires the Secure attribute on the cookie.
en.explanation: MDN says Secure must also be set with SameSite=None. Its compatibility data shows Chrome and Firefox rejecting a SameSite=None cookie that lacks Secure, while Safari does not enforce the rule.

en.statement: The __Secure- prefix also requires HttpOnly on the cookie.
en.explanation: In supporting browsers, __Secure- requires a secure page and the Secure attribute. The prefix does not require HttpOnly.

en.statement: In supporting browsers, a __Host- cookie omits Domain to bind it to its setting host.
en.explanation: The __Host- prefix forbids Domain in supporting browsers, preventing the cookie from being scoped to subdomains.

en.statement: Chrome blocks third-party cookies by default in regular windows.
en.explanation: MDN reports that Chrome permits third-party cookies by default in regular browsing. Its default differs from browsers that restrict them.

en.statement: Reflected XSS requires an application to save the attacker's payload before returning it.
en.explanation: OWASP describes Reflected XSS as unsafe request input returned immediately in a response, with no permanent storage of that input.

en.statement: Stored XSS can arise from attacker content saved in browser storage for later visits.
en.explanation: OWASP notes that stored XSS payloads may reside in the victim's browser storage as well as on a server.

en.statement: DOM-based XSS requires a changed server HTML response after the attacker supplies input.
en.explanation: With DOM-based XSS, unsafe client code reacts to changes in the browser's DOM environment; the server's HTML response can remain unchanged.

en.statement: OWASP's Client XSS includes cases involving reflected input and cases involving stored input.
en.explanation: OWASP's client/server terms describe where unsafe insertion happens. Client XSS can use either reflected or stored attacker input.

en.statement: Assigning attacker-controlled text to Node.textContent makes the browser parse it as HTML.
en.explanation: Node.textContent inserts text rather than interpreting it as HTML. OWASP recommends it for displaying untrusted data in the DOM.

source.title: DOM based XSS Prevention Cheat Sheet

en.statement: HTML escaping alone secures unquoted attribute values containing attacker input.
en.explanation: An unquoted attribute value can let attacker input introduce another attribute even when a template escapes HTML characters. Quote the value and encode for its context.

en.statement: An HTML sanitizer can remove an inline event handler while retaining its HTML element.
en.explanation: Sanitization can strip executable features such as event handlers from markup that an application intends to render as HTML.

en.statement: React's dangerouslySetInnerHTML sanitizes the supplied markup during insertion.
en.explanation: dangerouslySetInnerHTML inserts markup without applying normal output encoding. The developer needs to ensure that supplied HTML is safe.

en.statement: X-XSS-Protection is a recommended header for new web projects.
en.explanation: MDN marks X-XSS-Protection as deprecated and non-standard, advises against using it in new projects, and warns that it can introduce XSS flaws.

en.statement: An omitted img-src makes default-src govern image loads under a CSP.
en.explanation: When a policy includes default-src and omits img-src, the browser applies default-src to image fetches.

en.statement: The browser combines script-src-elem and script-src source lists for <script> elements.
en.explanation: An explicit script-src-elem supplies the policy for script elements. The browser falls back to script-src when script-src-elem is absent.

en.statement: A server uses a fresh CSP nonce in each response to allow selected inline scripts.
en.explanation: The server places a newly generated nonce in both the CSP and the selected script elements for each response.

en.statement: A CSP hash still matches an inline script after its whitespace changes.
en.explanation: A CSP hash covers the script's contents. A whitespace edit changes the content and calls for a newly calculated hash.

en.statement: 'strict-dynamic' passes trust from a nonce-authorized script to scripts it loads.
en.explanation: With 'strict-dynamic', a script authorized by a nonce or hash may load further scripts that lack their own nonce or hash.

en.statement: 'unsafe-inline' re-enables inline scripts alongside a nonce source in the same directive.
en.explanation: Browsers ignore 'unsafe-inline' in a directive containing a nonce or hash source.

en.statement: 'unsafe-eval' permits the Function() constructor under script-src.
en.explanation: CSP treats the Function() constructor as string-to-code execution. The 'unsafe-eval' keyword permits that behavior.

en.statement: report-to selects a named CSP endpoint defined by Reporting-Endpoints.
en.explanation: The Reporting-Endpoints response header defines a named URL, and the CSP report-to directive selects that name for violation reports.

en.statement: A browser that supports report-to also uses report-uri when one CSP sets both.
en.explanation: In a browser that supports report-to, report-uri is ignored when the policy also sets report-to, so reports go only to the report-to endpoint. report-uri is deprecated.

en.statement: An HTML meta element can deliver Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only.
en.explanation: A report-only CSP is delivered through the Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only HTTP response header, not an HTML meta element.

en.statement: A CSRF token set to the user's ID protects a form, since that value differs between users.
en.explanation: OWASP wants CSRF tokens secret and unpredictable, a large random value from a secure generator. A user ID is neither, so an attacker can put it in a forged request.

source.title: Cross-Site Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet - OWASP

en.statement: The server compares a synchronizer CSRF token with the value stored in the user's session.
en.explanation: In the synchronizer token pattern, the server checks the submitted token against the session's token and rejects a missing or mismatched value.

source.title: Cross-Site Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet

en.statement: A hidden form input carries a CSRF token back to the server on submission.
en.explanation: A server can place a CSRF token in a hidden form field and check the returned value when the form is submitted.

en.statement: A custom CSRF header on a cross-origin fetch() POST triggers a preflight.
en.explanation: A custom request header causes a cross-origin fetch() POST to require preflight approval, which the server can deny to untrusted origins.

en.statement: Content-Type: application/json makes a cross-origin fetch() POST skip preflight.
en.explanation: application/json is outside the Content-Type values that avoid CORS preflight. A cross-origin fetch() POST using it triggers a preflight.

en.statement: A custom-header CSRF defense holds when the API's CORS policy reflects any origin and allows credentials.
en.explanation: MDN warns that a site is open to CSRF from an origin when its response lists that origin in Access-Control-Allow-Origin and sends Access-Control-Allow-Credentials, as an origin-reflecting policy does.

en.statement: When Origin is missing, OWASP's origin check falls back to the hostname in the Referer header.
en.explanation: OWASP compares the Referer hostname with the target origin when a request lacks Origin, and recommends blocking a request that carries neither header.

source.title: Cross-Site Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet - OWASP

en.statement: Sec-Fetch-Site: none identifies a cross-site page as the request initiator.
en.explanation: Sec-Fetch-Site: none identifies a user-originated operation, such as opening a bookmark or entering a URL. A different-site initiator uses cross-site.

en.statement: A GET endpoint that changes account data avoids CSRF because it uses a safe HTTP method.
en.explanation: A state-changing GET endpoint is vulnerable to forgery through a cross-site link or resource load. GET requests should not change server state.

en.statement: A clickjacking page puts a transparent target iframe over a decoy button.
en.explanation: The victim sees the decoy but clicks a sensitive control in the transparent target page layered over it.

en.statement: frame-ancestors accepts several permitted parent origins in one CSP directive.
en.explanation: A frame-ancestors source list can name multiple parents permitted to embed the protected document.

en.statement: frame-ancestors 'none' permits a same-origin page to embed the protected page.
en.explanation: frame-ancestors 'none' prevents embedding by any parent, including one from the protected page's own origin.

en.statement: default-src 'none' in a CSP blocks framing when frame-ancestors is omitted.
en.explanation: frame-ancestors has no default-src fallback. A policy containing only default-src 'none' does not restrict who embeds the page.

en.statement: X-Frame-Options governs whether a browser renders a page inside an <embed> or <object>.
en.explanation: The header tells the browser whether the document may render in a <frame>, <iframe>, <embed> or <object>, so it covers more than iframes.

en.statement: X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN checks just the immediate parent in nested frames.
en.explanation: SAMEORIGIN requires every ancestor frame to share the protected page's origin, not merely its immediate parent.

en.statement: Modern browsers enforce X-Frame-Options: ALLOW-FROM for the named origin.
en.explanation: ALLOW-FROM is obsolete. Modern browsers that encounter it ignore the entire X-Frame-Options header.

en.statement: An HTML meta element makes X-Frame-Options: DENY effective for that page.
en.explanation: Browsers enforce X-Frame-Options from an HTTP response header. Placing it in a meta element has no effect.

en.statement: A browser applying an enforced frame-ancestors policy also applies X-Frame-Options.
en.explanation: A browser that supports and enforces frame-ancestors ignores X-Frame-Options for that response.

en.statement: SameSite=Lax keeps a session cookie out of a cross-site iframe, limiting clickjacking.
en.explanation: A cross-site framed page lacks that Lax session cookie, weakening attacks that need an authenticated victim. This is a partial mitigation.

en.statement: A CORS-enabled mirror serving byte-identical script fails the SRI hash made for the CDN copy.
en.explanation: SRI hashes the fetched contents, not the URL or host, so identical bytes match the same integrity value wherever they are served from.

en.statement: SRI integrity values accept sha256-, sha384-, and sha512- digest prefixes.
en.explanation: The prefix identifies which SHA-2 algorithm the browser uses when checking the resource's digest.

en.statement: An SRI digest after its algorithm prefix may use hexadecimal encoding.
en.explanation: The digest in an integrity value uses Base64 encoding, not the hexadecimal form commonly printed by hash tools.

en.statement: A matching sha256- hash can validate a resource even when its sha512- hash differs.
en.explanation: When integrity lists SHA-256 and SHA-512 hashes, the browser checks the SHA-512 entries and ignores the weaker SHA-256 entries.

en.statement: Two sha384- hashes in one integrity value allow either matching resource version.
en.explanation: When several hashes use the strongest listed algorithm, a match with any one of those hashes validates the resource.

en.statement: A cross-origin SRI script uses crossorigin="anonymous" to request CORS mode.
en.explanation: The crossorigin attribute changes the cross-origin script fetch from its usual no-cors mode to CORS mode for integrity checking.

en.statement: For cross-origin SRI, a matching hash replaces the need for Access-Control-Allow-Origin.
en.explanation: A cross-origin SRI load also needs the resource server to pass the CORS check, using an appropriate Access-Control-Allow-Origin response header.

en.statement: A browser returns a network error when an SRI digest fails to match the response.
en.explanation: The browser refuses the fetched resource when none of the applicable integrity hashes matches its contents.

en.statement: A <script src> element accepts integrity metadata for its external script.
en.explanation: A script element with src can carry an integrity attribute for checking the fetched script.

en.statement: SRI applies to <link> resources with rel=stylesheet, rel=preload, or rel=modulepreload.
en.explanation: MDN lists stylesheet, preload, and modulepreload as link relationships whose fetched resources can use integrity metadata.

en.statement: An HTTPS iframe embedded by an HTTP top-level page remains a secure context.
en.explanation: A framed HTTPS document needs a secure embedding parent to be a secure context. An HTTP top-level parent prevents that.

en.statement: A top-level http://localhost page qualifies as a secure context.
en.explanation: Browsers treat localhost as potentially trustworthy, so a top-level page there can use APIs restricted to secure contexts.

en.statement: An HTTPS page upgrades an HTTP <script src> request before executing the script.
en.explanation: An HTTP script requested by an HTTPS page is blockable mixed content. The browser blocks the request rather than upgrading it.

en.statement: An HTTPS page upgrades HTTP image URLs whose host is an IP address.
en.explanation: Browsers block an HTTP image URL with an IP-address host instead of applying the usual image upgrade.

en.statement: Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=0 over HTTPS clears the HSTS policy a browser stored for the host.
en.explanation: Setting max-age=0 is how a site turns HSTS off: the browser removes the HSTS policy it had stored for that host.

en.statement: A browser acts on a Strict-Transport-Security header only when the header arrives over HTTPS.
en.explanation: Browsers ignore the header on plain-HTTP responses, so a manipulator in the middle cannot add it for a host or make it expire early.

en.statement: A preloaded HSTS host can avoid an insecure first visit before receiving its own HSTS header.
en.explanation: A browser with the host in its HSTS preload list starts with HTTPS even before it has received that site's header.

en.statement: The default Referrer-Policy sends only the origin on an HTTPS-to-HTTPS cross-origin request.
en.explanation: The current default, strict-origin-when-cross-origin, sends an origin rather than a full URL to another HTTPS origin.

en.statement: Under Referrer-Policy: no-referrer, a cross-origin fetch() POST in the default cors mode sends Origin: null.
en.explanation: A cors-mode request that sends Origin carries its real origin whatever the referrer policy; no-referrer sets Origin to null only for non-GET, non-HEAD requests in other modes, such as form posts.
